title: LCIA Challenge Decision — Decision 6 (06/09/2018)
text:
DECISION RENDERED ON 6 SEPTEMBER 2018
Subject: The Third Respondent challenged the entire Tribunal (entirely selected by the
LCIA Court) pursuant to Article 10.3 of the LCIA Rules 2014.
Outcome: Rejected
Seat: London, England
Governing Law of English law
the Contract:
Summary: The challenge related to procedural decisions made by the Tribunal.
The LCIA Court rejected the challenge.
The LCIA Court applied the LCIA Rules as the procedural rules applicable in the
proceedings together with the English Arbitration Act 1996 on the basis that
London was the place of arbitration.
While the Third Respondent relied upon a Partial Award as the “culmination”
of some of its grounds for challenge, certain objections related to earlier
events. Insofar as the Third Respondent sought to challenge the Tribunal on
the basis of events prior to the Partial Award, such a challenge was out of time.
The LCIA Court, therefore, confined its consideration of each such ground to
an assessment of whether the content (or lack of content) in the Partial Award
itself gave rise to justifiable doubts as to the Tribunal members’ impartiality
or independence, or whether the Partial Award reflected or demonstrated a
failure to act fairly or impartially as between the Parties.
For a violation of due process in arbitration proceedings to give rise to doubts
as to an arbitrator’s impartiality or independence, or amount to a failure to
act fairly or impartially, such a violation (or series of violations) “would have
to possess a certain gravity or level of seriousness.”
The Tribunal’s refusal to draw an adverse inference in the Partial Award on
the basis of the late disclosure of certain documents is not unfair, nor does it
give rise to doubts as to the Tribunal members’ impartiality. The Tribunal
weighed the evidence before it and reached the conclusion that the inference
sought was “inconsistent with the available evidence”.
The fact that the Tribunal did not exercise its power under Article 18.6 of the
LCIA Rules (regarding sanctions of legal representatives) or failed to refer to a
request to do so in the Partial Award, displays no preference for any party.

The Tribunal’s indication that certain late documents submitted by the Fifth
Respondent would be considered only if the Claimant had sufficient
opportunity to address them is not indicative of bias.
The absence in the Partial Award of reasons for admitting certain late
documents, or sanctions upon the Claimant for its late submission of
documents, does not give rise to doubts about the Tribunal’s impartiality or
independence.
The Tribunal’s email seeking clarification and supplementation from the
Claimant with respect to certain aspects of documents submitted does not
evidence any bias, and no explanation or justification for such clarification was
required. The Tribunal is entitled to question the Parties regarding the
evidence before it as it sees fit, to assist it in ascribing the weight it deems
appropriate to such evidence.
The Tribunal’s failure to address explicitly one argument made by a Party in its
submissions did not reach the gravity necessary to give rise to doubts about
the Tribunal’s impartiality or independence.
A challenge is not the proper forum to make a determination regarding the
Tribunal’s power to refer to legal authorities outside those cited by the parties,
or to debate the legal principle of “jura novit curia”.
The Tribunal’s failure to address, in the Partial Award, conduct allegedly
relevant to the future distribution of costs is not indicative of any bias.
The Tribunal’s confirmation of receipt of an email from a Party concerning a
proposed procedural order when the Tribunal had in fact not received that
email was clearly a mere oversight and not deliberate or reflective of any bias,
particularly when the Tribunal’s resulting order was consistent with that
Party’s view and not adverse to it in any way.
The Tribunal’s ex parte communication with a Party regarding the contact
information of another Party, while it constitutes a regrettable oversight, is
not evidence of bias, considering that the failure to copy the other Parties was
remedied as soon as the Tribunal was alerted to it.

I. PROCEDURE
1. On 15 January 2018, the LCIA Court informed the Parties that it had appointed [A], [B] and [C] as
members of the arbitral tribunal in LCIA Case No. […] (“the Tribunal”).
2. On 31 May 2018, the Tribunal rendered a Partial Award on Jurisdiction (“Partial Award”). The Partial
Award was transmitted to the Parties by the LCIA on 11 June 2018.
3. On 25 June 2018, Third Respondent submitted a challenge to all three members of the Tribunal
(“Challenge”), invoking Articles 10.1 (iii) and 10.2 (ii) of the LCIA Arbitration Rules effective 1 October
2014 (“LCIA Rules”). Together with the Challenge, Third Respondent filed Annex 1, entitled “The Table
on Correspondence between the Parties and the Tribunal” and exhibits numbered 1 to 34 (herein
referred to as “Exhibits R3-1 to R3-34”).

4. On 28 June 2018, Claimant objected to the Challenge, and offered to provide brief written submissions
in response.
5. On 12 July 2018, the LCIA Court appointed [D] to decide upon the Challenge […] (“Undersigned”).
6. On 20 July 2018, the Undersigned set a procedural timetable to provide the other Parties and the
challenged arbitrators with the opportunity to comment upon the Challenge, pursuant to Article 10.4
of the LCIA Rules.
7. On 25 July 2018, Third Respondent emailed the Undersigned, copying the other Parties and the
Tribunal, indicating that it would like to supplement the Challenge with two further grounds.
According to Third Respondent, these two additional grounds:
. . . reinforce the Third Respondent’s position that under Article 10.2(iii) of the LCIA Rules, all members
of the Tribunal are “unfit to act under Article 10.1” because they have not acted “fairly and impartially
as between all parties.
8. On 26 July 2018, in light of Third Respondent’s email of 25 July 2018, the Undersigned adjusted the
timetable for the Parties’ and the Tribunal’s comments and respective replies on the Challenge. The
revised timetable was as follows:
(a) Comments on the Challenge, if any, by Claimant, First Respondent, Second
Respondent, Fourth Respondent, and Fifth Respondent: by Friday, 3 August 2018.
(b) Comments on the Challenge, if any, by the Members of the Tribunal, i.e. [A], [B] and
[C]: by Wednesday, 8 August 2018.
(c) Reply comments, if any, by the challenging Party, i.e. Third Respondent: by
Monday, 13 August 2018.
(d) Rejoinder comments, if any, by Claimant, First Respondent, Second Respondent,
Fourth Respondent, Fifth Respondent and by the Members of the Tribunal, i.e. [A],
[B] and [C]: by Friday, 17 August 2018.
9. On 27 July 2018, Claimant stated by email that:
it is regrettable that the Third Respondent should again, as with the Jurisdiction Challenge, present
another challenge to the Tribunal in such an incremental fashion, but the Claimant is prepared to

address these further grounds briefly in its written submissions in response to the bias and impartiality
challenge.
10. On 3 August 2018, Claimant submitted its comments on the Challenge (“Claimant’s Comments”).
11. No comments on the Challenge were received from First Respondent, Second Respondent, Fourth
Respondent or Fifth Respondent.
12. On 7 August 2018, the Tribunal submitted its comments on the Challenge (“Tribunal’s Comments”).
13. On 13 August 2018, Third Respondent submitted its reply to the comments of Claimant and the
Tribunal regarding the Challenge (“Third Respondent’s Reply Comments”), together with exhibits
numbered 35 to 50 (herein referred to as “Exhibits R3-35 to R3-50”).
14. On 16 August 2018, the Tribunal Chair indicated, on behalf of the Tribunal, that the Tribunal has no
further comments on the Challenge, referring to its position as set out in its directions and orders, the
Partial Award, and its comments of 7 August 2018.
15. On 17 August 2018, Claimant submitted its rejoinder comments on the Challenge (“Claimant’s
Rejoinder Comments”).
16. Taking into account the Tribunal’s order dated 17 July 2018 pursuant to Articles 4.2 and 4.3 of the LCIA
Rules, the communications mentioned at ¶¶ 6 and 8 above were also delivered by hard copy to Second
and Fourth Respondent at their primary and alternative addresses.
17. In Section II below, the Undersigned will set out the legal standard relevant to the determination of
the Challenge. Section III contains the analysis of each ground, including the facts relevant to the
Challenge, the Parties’ and the Tribunal’s positions, and the determination with respect to each
ground for the Challenge.
Decision 6 - 5

II. LEGAL STANDARD
18. The legal standard relevant to the determination of this Challenge is not in dispute.1 The Undersigned
will apply the LCIA Rules, as the procedural rules applicable in these proceedings, together with the
English Arbitration Act 1996 (“Arbitration Act”), on the basis that London is the place of arbitration.
19. Article 10 of the LCIA Rules provides as follows:
10.1 The LCIA Court may revoke any arbitrator’s appointment upon its own initiative, at the written
request of all other members of the Arbitral Tribunal or upon a written challenge by any party if: (i)
that arbitrator gives written notice to the LCIA Court of his or her intent to resign as arbitrator, to be
copied to all parties and all other members of the Arbitral Tribunal (if any); (ii) that arbitrator falls
seriously ill, refuses or becomes unable or unfit to act; or (iii) circumstances exist that give rise to
justifiable doubts as to that arbitrator’s impartiality or independence.
10.2 The LCIA Court may determine that an arbitrator is unfit to act under Article 10.1 if that arbitrator:
(i) acts in deliberate violation of the Arbitration Agreement; (ii) does not act fairly or impartially as
between the parties; or (iii) does not conduct or participate in the arbitration with reasonable
efficiency, diligence and industry.
10.3 A party challenging an arbitrator under Article 10.1 shall, within 14 days of the formation of the
Arbitral Tribunal or (if later) within 14 days of becoming aware of any grounds described in Article
10.1 or 10.2, deliver a written statement of the reasons for its challenge to the LCIA Court, the Arbitral
Tribunal and all other parties. A party may challenge an arbitrator whom it has nominated, or in whose
appointment it has participated, only for reasons of which it becomes aware after the appointment
has been made by the LCIA Court.
10.4 The LCIA Court shall provide to those other parties and the challenged arbitrator a reasonable
opportunity to comment on the challenging party’s written statement. The LCIA Court may require at
any time further information and materials from the challenging party, the challenged arbitrator,
other parties and other members of the Arbitral Tribunal (if any).
10.5 If all other parties agree in writing to the challenge within 14 days of receipt of the written
statement, the LCIA Court shall revoke that arbitrator’s appointment (without reasons).
10.6 Unless the parties so agree or the challenged arbitrator resigns in writing within 14 days of
receipt of the written statement, the LCIA Court shall decide the challenge and, if upheld, shall revoke
that arbitrator’s appointment. The LCIA Court’s decision shall be made in writing, with reasons; and a
copy shall be transmitted by the Registrar to the parties, the challenged arbitrator and other members
of the Arbitral Tribunal (if any). A challenged arbitrator who resigns in writing prior to the LCIA Court’s
decision shall not be considered as having admitted any part of the written statement.
1 Challenge, ¶¶ 8-19; Claimant’s Comments, ¶ 10; Tribunal’s Comments, ¶ 2.

10.7 The LCIA Court shall determine the amount of fees and expenses (if any) to be paid for the former
arbitrator’s services, as it may consider appropriate in the circumstances. The LCIA Court may also
determine whether, in what amount and to whom any party should pay forthwith the costs of the
challenge; and the LCIA Court may also refer all or any part of such costs to the later decision of the
Arbitral Tribunal and/or the LCIA Court under Article 28.
20. Sections 24(1)(a) and 33(1)(a) and of the Arbitration Act further provide:
24 Power of court to remove arbitrator.
(1) A party to arbitral proceedings may (upon notice to the other parties, to the arbitrator concerned
and to any other arbitrator) apply to the court to remove an arbitrator on any of the following grounds
–
(a) that circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as to his impartiality[.]
. . . .
33 General duty of the tribunal
(1) The tribunal shall –
(a) act fairly and impartially as between the parties, giving each party a reasonable opportunity of
putting his case and dealing with that of his opponent.
21. There are two elements of the above provisions which have been invoked by Third Respondent: (i) the
duty to act fairly and impartially between the Parties; and (ii) whether circumstances exist that give
rise to justifiable doubts as to the arbitrators’ impartiality or independence.
22. The right to be heard by an independent and impartial tribunal is further reinforced by Article 6(1) of
the European Convention on Human Rights, which became part of English law following the passage
of the Human Rights Act 1998.
23. The standard to determine whether there are “justifiable doubts” as to an arbitrator’s impartiality or
independence under the Arbitration Act is further elaborated in English case law. Since the standard
under the Arbitration Act is similar to the standard under the LCIA Rules (save that the Act refers only
to impartiality and not, as the Rules, also to independence), this case law will also be taken into
account. In this respect, the relevant test is set out in the Gough case, as modified by Magill v. Porter.
The test is an objective one, and inquires:
Decision 6 - 7

[w]hether the fair-minded and informed observer, having considered the facts, would conclude that
there was a real possibility that the tribunal was biased.2
24. The applicable test seeks to determine whether there is a “real possibility” of bias, as opposed to
actual bias. Moreover, “what is decisive is whether any fears expressed by the complainer are
objectively justified”,3 and “not . . . whether the arbitrator did or did not in fact allow his mind to be
affected” by the relevant circumstances.4
25. As pointed out by Third Respondent, English courts often proceed by a two step analysis. First, they
examine the relevant circumstances to determine whether they give rise to doubts regarding an
arbitrator’s impartiality. If so, the second step is to determine whether those circumstances would
objectively lead one to conclude that there was a “reasonable possibility”, i.e. “justifiable doubts”,
that the arbitrator was biased.5 In case of real ground for doubt, it should be resolved in favour of
recusal.6 Article 10.1(iii) of the LCIA Rules modifies the test under English law by providing for a
challenge if circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as to the arbitrator’s independence,
and not just his or her impartiality.
26. Taking into account this legal standard, the Undersigned proceeds to examine the substance of the
Challenge, and in particular whether (i) circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as to the
impartiality or independence of any member of the Tribunal; or (ii) any member of the Tribunal failed
to act fairly or impartially as between the Parties.
III. ANALYSIS
27. In its Challenge, Third Respondent originally included eight grounds as the basis for its Challenge. By
its email dated 25 July 2018 (see ¶ 7 above), Third Respondent sought to introduce two further
grounds for the Challenge (“Challenge Supplement”). Subject to the considerations below regarding
the timeliness and merits of these two additional grounds, the Undersigned shall address those two
grounds as grounds nine and ten, together with the Challenge as a whole.
2 Magill v. Porter [2001] UKHL 67, ¶ 103, per Lord Hope.
3 Ibid., ¶ 104.
4 Rustal Trading Limited v. Gill & Duffus S.A. WL 1142684 [1999], per The Hon. Mr. Justice Moore-Bick.
5 Ibid.
6 Locabail (UK) v. Bayfield Properties Ltd [2000] 1 All ER 65, ¶ 77.
Decision 6 - 8

28. In the subsections that follow, the Undersigned will set forth the relevant facts relating to each alleged
ground for the Challenge. Under each ground, the Undersigned will also summarise the Parties’ and
the Tribunal’s respective positions regarding that ground. For convenience, the analysis of the
Undersigned with respect to each ground is set out after the relevant positions. Notwithstanding this
ground-by-ground analysis, Section 10 below contains an assessment of the grounds of the Challenge
as a whole.
29. The numerous detailed arguments made by the Parties and the Tribunal have been considered in
reaching the determinations herein. To the extent that an argument from the written submissions is
not referred to expressly, it is subsumed into the Undersigned’s analysis.
30. Since the Challenge is made to all three members of the Tribunal, and the Parties’ submissions
generally make reference to the Tribunal as a whole, in this decision the Undersigned also refers to
the “Tribunal” as including all three members without distinction, unless otherwise indicated.
1. Ground 1: Admission of Documents Filed on 27 February 2018 and 14 March 2018
(a) Facts
31. On 15 February 2018, following an application by Third Respondent, the Tribunal issued Procedural
Order No. 1 (“PO 1”). Among other things, PO 1 partially granted an application by Third Respondent,
ordering Claimant to disclose “all documents upon which it relies as demonstrating its title to claim as
assignee and invoke the arbitration clause in this matter”. The remainder of Third Respondent’s
application, which had requested the disclosure of other documents, was denied.7
32. On 21 February 2018, the Partial Award records (and it appears undisputed) that Claimant disclosed
documents CJ1 to CJ21, pursuant to PO 1.8
33. On 26 February 2018, Third Respondent commented on Claimant’s document production of 21
February 2018, alleging that Claimant had failed to produce crucial documents in its possession that
it had been ordered to disclose, in breach of PO 1. Third Respondent requested the Tribunal to order

Claimant to produce all documents “that would demonstrate the corporate structure of the Claimant
/ its connection with both [Entity 1] and [Entity 2]”.9
34. On 27 February 2018, the Tribunal denied Third Respondent’s request, stating as follows:
Paragraph 2 of PO1 sufficiently covers what is required from the Claimant to demonstrate its title and,
indeed, the Third Respondent has already put the Claimant on notice of what it says are deficiencies
in the Claimant’s disclosure to date.
The Tribunal considers that since the burden is on the Claimant to establish its title clearly, the existing
procedure is sufficient to accommodate the Third Respondent’s concerns. Ultimately, it is the
Claimant that bears the burden of any adverse consequences arising from a failure to establish its right
to invoke the arbitration clause. Accordingly, the Tribunal sees no need at the present time to amend
its disclosure order or the timetable for the Parties’ written submissions.
Should the Claimant produce any new documents in response to the Third Respondent’s submissions
due on 20 March 2018 which the Third Respondent considers it cannot adequately address in its oral
submissions at the hearing on 28 March 2018, it may make such application as it considers necessary
at that time.10
35. Also on 27 February 2018, in response to Third Respondent’s email of 26 February 2018, Claimant
alleged that Third Respondent “has now raised a further basis for challenge” of the Tribunal’s
jurisdiction, that had not been raised previously. Claimant attached to the email, “by way of further,
voluntary disclosure”, four documents numbered CJ22-CJ25.11
36. On the same date, in response to Claimant’s email, the Tribunal stated:
I acknowledge receipt of your email letter of this afternoon, the points there made are noted and will
doubtless be addressed by Respondents in due course.12
37. On 6 March 2018, in its Memorial on Objections to Jurisdiction, Third Respondent submitted that
Claimant had “failed to discharge its burden to prove its title to invoke the arbitration agreement
under the […] Agreement . . .”, and contended that “all adverse inferences in this regard should be
drawn against the Claimant”.13

38. On 14 March 2018, citing Third Respondent’s request for the Tribunal to draw adverse inferences,
Claimant stated that “upon further investigation in response to the additional contentions” of Third
Respondent, it had “identified four further documents in its possession which it considers ought to be
disclosed for completeness and in order to assist the Tribunal with the determination of the new
issues”.14 Claimant attached documents CJ26-CJ29 to its email.
39. On 15 March 2018, the Tribunal indicated that:
[t]he Respondents may comment upon all the Claimant’s jurisdiction disclosure as previously directed.
If any difficulties arise these should be brought to the attention of the Tribunal at the earliest
opportunity.15
40. Also on 15 March 2018, Third Respondent commented on Claimant’s disclosure, requesting among
other things (i) the Tribunal to put on record “Claimant’s deliberate breach of paragraph 3 of the PO1”,
due to the late submission of the documents CJ26-CJ29, which deprived Respondents of their right to
comment on them in their written submissions; and (ii) the Tribunal to grant “reasonable deadlines”
for Respondents to comment on new documents. Third Respondent further contended that in its view,
Respondents’ proposals with respect to the procedural timetable have not been taken into account
by the Tribunal in PO 1 and further directions.16
41. On 16 March 2018, Claimant responded to Third Respondent’s email of 15 March 2018, contending
with respect to the new documents provided on 27 February 2018 (see paragraph 35 above) and 14
March 2018 (see paragraph 38 above) that they did not fall within the scope of PO 1. Claimant asserted
that only the documents filed on 21 February 2018 related to the directions in PO 1 (see paragraph 32
above). According to Claimant, the further disclosures on 27 February 2018 and 14 March 2018 “were
voluntarily provided by the Claimant to assist the Tribunal more quickly to dispose of several ill-
founded points raised late by the Third Respondent”.17
42. Also on 16 March 2018, the Tribunal referred to the correspondence in paragraphs 40-41 above and
addressed the Parties as follows:18

The Tribunal has considered the matters raised in the Third Respondent’s email of 15 March 2018
(below) and the Claimant’s response of today.
First, the Tribunal wishes to make it absolutely clear that it requires each Party to have had a real
opportunity of putting its case.
For that reason it has permitted documents to be presented by the Claimant even though later than
stipulated, and for expert evidence to be presented in support of a response to a challenge, even
though expert evidence was not originally expected.
Equally, each Respondent must be allowed to present its challenge fully.
The Third Respondent should therefore inform the Tribunal
* with regard to the Claimant’s New Documents, by which date it is reasonably able to present its
written reply,
* with regard to Cayman law expert evidence on the point raised by the Third Respondent itself, by
which date it can reasonably present this, counting from the date of receipt of such evidence by the
Third Respondent from the Claimant.
As regards the hearing on 28 March 2018, the Tribunal has not received notice from the Third
Respondent that it cannot attend, nor an application for a different date, but rather understands that
the Third Respondent prefers to make submissions in writing and does not consider an oral hearing
necessary. If the Third Respondent now takes a different view, the Tribunal will consider such view.
All Parties are reminded that there are 2 distinct jurisdiction challenges, namely the construction issue
and the assignment issue.
It was considered desirable to deal with both together.
If the assignment issue has become increasingly complex and if any of the Parties can genuinely not
be ready to address this by 28 March, be it orally or in writing, the Tribunal would be prepared to
determine the construction issue after the hearing on 28 March, and to determine the assignment
issue as part of the merits of the case should the construction challenge be resolved in favour of the
Claimant.
The Tribunal would of course prefer to offer resolution of both jurisdiction challenges together, at the
same time, but not if there is a genuine danger of a Party not being able to present its case.
In order to avoid prejudice to anyone, the Tribunal does not require to see precise reasons for why a
Party cannot properly address the assignment issue by or on 28 March 2018.
43. On 20 March 2018, Claimant submitted its Response to Respondents’ Objections to Jurisdiction.19

44. On 22 March 2018, Third Respondent indicated that it “would like to present its challenge fully and
have an opportunity to provide its comments to new legal issues and arguments as well as new
evidence” (emphasis in original). It requested, among other things, two weeks to prepare its
comments regarding “Claimant’s new legal issues and arguments, New Documents, and Cayman law
expert evidence”.20
45. On 22 March 2018, the Partial Award records that the Tribunal issued the following directions
regarding Third Respondent’s request:
. . . the Tribunal will consider written submissions and any expert report presented by the Third
Respondent by 14 days from today, namely on or before 5 April 2018, but does invite the Third

46. On 26 March 2018, the Tribunal rescheduled the hearing (originally scheduled for 28 March 2018) to

48. In the Partial Award, the Tribunal found as follows with respect to the evidence on assignment:
As for any alleged assignment agreements underlying the antecedent [documents], the Tribunal is
satisfied that the Claimant has made reasonable efforts to obtain these, as evidenced by its

Third Respondent is not justified in this case.25

49. On 18 April 2018, Fifth Respondent submitted a “brief supplement to written submission in support
of challenge of jurisdiction”, including legal authorities.26
50. On 19 April 2018, the Tribunal addressed the Parties as follows, in relevant part:
By #4 of its Direction of 26 March 2018 (hearing bundle C tabl 14B), the Tribunal stated that it expected
all written submissions to have been exchanged by 17 April 2018.
Two case reports were submitted by email yesterday, 18 April 2018, by the Fifth Respondents.
The Tribunal awaits hearing from the Claimant, but would be prepared to consider these two cases if
the Claimant has sufficient opportunity to address them, which may be done orally at the hearing.27
(b) Third Respondent’s Position
51. According to Third Respondent, the admission of Claimant’s late submissions of documents to the
record, in breach of the deadlines set in PO 1, casts doubt on the Tribunal’s impartiality, since (i)
Claimant did not seek, nor was it expressly granted, leave to file the documents; (ii) Respondents were
not invited to comment on the admission of the documents; (iii) the late submissions prejudiced Third
Respondent’s right to present its case, “given the extremely tight deadlines established by the Tribunal
upon the Claimant’s request”; (iv) the Tribunal did not respond to Third Respondent’s objections nor
are they reflected in the Partial Award.28
52. In Third Respondent’s view, the acceptance of Claimant’s late submissions is not justified by Claimant’s
right to be heard, but rather violates the Parties’ right to due process and a fair proceeding, which
requires respect for the time limits set by the Tribunal.29
53. Third Respondent further contends that the Tribunal treated the Parties differently. In this regard,
while the Tribunal “constantly permitted the Claimant’s late submissions”, Third Respondent argues
that the Tribunal was only prepared to consider Fifth Respondent’s submission of 18 April 2018 (see
paragraphs 49-50 above) “if the Claimant has sufficient opportunity to address” it.30 Third Respondent

submits that contrary to the Tribunal’s contention, only Claimant was invited to comment on Fifth

54. In light of Claimant’s disclosure of 27 February 2018 (see paragraph 35 above), Third Respondent
submits that the Tribunal should have (i) not admitted the new documents, or (ii) if admitted, put the
Claimant’s violation on record, and/or (iii) amended the existing procedure for Third Respondent to
put its case. In any event, Third Respondent contends that the Tribunal should have made a decision
on adverse inferences, and ruled on Claimant’s actions in breach of PO 1 in the Partial Award.32
55. While the Tribunal did address the issue of adverse inferences in the Partial Award, Third Respondent
